title: A tree of life (Proverbs 3:17–18)
hook: sung as the Torah returns to the ark: "Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mishlei opened with its foundation: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. Can you still say it without looking? Your line was the beginning of knowledge. Today, two verses from the same book that left the page and became a song. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

The reading is over. The scroll has been lifted, rolled and dressed again in its cover. It's carried back toward the ark at the front of the synagogue, and the doors stand open. As it goes in, the congregation sings. The song's opening lines aren't new words written for the moment. They're two verses lifted straight out of the book of Proverbs. Wisdom and Torah, sung in one breath, and then the doors close on the scroll.
screen: `THE READING IS OVER.` → `THE SCROLL RETURNS TO THE ARK.` → `TWO VERSES FROM PROVERBS.`

segments.voice: Here are the verses, in the words of the King James text. "She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her." And just before it: "Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace." In Proverbs, the she is wisdom. The chapter describes her like a person: more precious than rubies, with long life in one hand and riches and honor in the other. Wisdom is someone to walk beside. Then the synagogue does something quiet and bold. It sings those verses about the Torah. As the scroll goes back into the ark, wisdom and Torah are heard as one. The Torah becomes the tree, and the people singing are the ones holding on. Notice the verb: lay hold upon her. A tree of life isn't something you admire from a distance. You grab it. You hold on. The tradition gives this a physical shape too: the wooden rollers a Torah scroll is wound on are called atzei chayim, trees of life. Every time someone lifts the scroll, their hands are literally on the trees. And then the second verse. Her ways are ways of pleasantness. Some Jewish teachers have used this line as a test: in the Talmud, a reading of the law that would bring needless hardship is set aside, because her ways are pleasant. All her paths are peace. Peace here is shalom, a word with room in it for wholeness, for things being as they should be. So the song asks a lot of the people who sing it. Hold on to the tree. And choose the path that leads to peace.
screen: `WISDOM, LIKE A PERSON.` · `SUNG AS THE TORAH RETURNS.` · then, large: `SHE IS A TREE OF LIFE.` · then: `ALL HER PATHS ARE PEACE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to take the pleasant path once. Let one choice from today come to mind: a message to answer, a chore, a conversation, a line at the store. Picture two ways through it. One sharper, one gentler. You don't have to decide now. Just see both clearly. Then let your hands close lightly, as if holding on to something steady. If you pray, you can say the line silently: all her paths are peace. If not, just breathe and hold the picture. The bell holds the time.
A tree of life. In Proverbs, wisdom; in the synagogue, the Torah; and the name of the wooden rollers people hold when they lift the scroll. Today's word.
Your line: all her paths are peace. Today, when you reach a fork, sharp or gentle, take the gentler path once, and notice what follows. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: In synagogue services, as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark, congregations sing Etz chayim hi, the verses from Proverbs 3:18 and 3:17, before the ark is closed.

notes: Proverbs 3:17–18 quoted from the KJV; JPS 1917 wording should match these clauses, but Keeper please confirm.
Claims about liturgy (Etz chayim hi sung as the Torah returns to the ark, 'among the last words sung' in many services) come from the outline; Keeper please confirm wording across rites.
atzei chayim as the name of the Torah scroll's rollers: Keeper please confirm.
'Her ways are ways of pleasantness' used as an interpretive principle (e.g. in Talmudic discussion) is stated as 'some Jewish teachers'; Keeper please confirm framing and consider a citation.
Pronunciation עץ חיים given as etz khah-YEEM.

Audit: 'a reading that leads to cruelty can't be right' overstated the principle; the Talmud uses 'her ways are ways of pleasantness' to set aside readings that would cause needless hardship (e.g. Sukkah 32b on the myrtle, Yevamot 87b). Teach and trapdoor now say that, with the Talmud cited. Practice no longer asks for open hands 'as if holding on' (a contradiction).

Editor: the hymn sung as the ark closes continues past Proverbs (it ends with Lamentations 5:21, 'Turn thou us unto thee'); hook and myth now say its opening lines come from Proverbs rather than implying the whole song does.
